title: Rising Rivalry in the Gulf — Eddie Would Go
units: G E O P O L I T I C S · E N E R G Y · P E R S I A N G U L F · 20 min read
Rising rivalry in the Gulf.
Abu Dhabi · May 2026 · Geopolitics · Energy · Persian Gulf
«So as not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that fortune is the arbiter of one half of our actions, but that she still leaves the direction of the other half, or almost, to us.»
— Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, Chapter XXV

On the night of 28 February 2026, as the first missiles of Operation Epic Fury crossed the sky over Tehran, a different light lit up the screens of the crisis rooms in Abu Dhabi. It was not the light of the fire, though Iran was burning. It was the cold light of oil production models, updated in real time by ADNOC's engineers. Mohamed bin Zayed, the man who over a decade had built the most sophisticated state in the Arab world, looked at two numbers with concentration: 4.8 million barrels of daily capacity. 3.2 million OPEC quota. The difference between them — 1.6 million barrels, equivalent to Ecuador's entire energy GDP — was his prisoner. And now, while the world burned, the cell door stood open.

On 28 April, the UAE announced its departure from OPEC and OPEC+ with immediate effect. The energy minister, Suhail Al Mazrouei, communicated it without consulting Riyadh. "It is a sovereign national decision", he said. Translated from the diplomatic language of the Gulf: Mohammed bin Salman found out through the newspapers.

But this move did not emerge overnight. It was the last visible act of a fracture that had been cooking for years across four Arab battlefields: Yemen, Sudan, Libya and the Horn of Africa. In each of those conflicts, the UAE and Saudi Arabia ended up backing different sides. The accumulated geopolitical collision has hollowed out the strategic relationship until it is unrecognisable. The OPEC exit was not a rupture; it was the death certificate of an alignment that had been dead for some time.
The perfect timing

There is an elegant cruelty in the moment chosen. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil passes, has been closed for weeks. Gulf exports are strangled. OPEC production collapsed by 27 per cent in March — 7.88 million barrels a day less, a contraction exceeding the 1973 embargo and the 1991 Gulf War. In that context, the Emirati exit has zero market impact today. Rystad's analysts said it without ambiguity: with the strait shut, everyone is equally imprisoned. Leaving now costs nothing.

But when Hormuz reopens, the UAE will be on the other side of the finish line. Free. With a target of 5 million barrels a day by 2027, without a quota, without a veto, without the interminable committee diplomacy that has defined its last two decades in the cartel. Al Mazrouei told CNN: "When the conflict ends, we expect to produce everything we can."
"Waiting your turn inside a quota system starts to look like leaving money on the table."
— Jorge León, Rystad Energy
The fracture that had been cooking

To understand what happened, one has to go back further than December. The fracture between MBZ and MBS was not born of oil. It was born of an ideological difference over what kind of regional order they wanted to build, and that difference manifested first in the wars others were fighting on their behalf.

The political scientist Guido Steinberg, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, put it precisely: the Arab Spring of 2011 was the year Abu Dhabi decided it could not depend on Washington — or on Riyadh — to protect its regional order. The electoral winners of the chaos were, in every case, movements of political Islam. In Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood. In Tunisia, Ennahda. In Libya, factions linked to the same network. In Yemen, the Islah party. For Abu Dhabi, organised political Islam was the principal existential threat. Not for theological reasons but for reasons of power: Brotherhood movements offer an alternative model of legitimacy that depends neither on oil wealth nor on royal houses.

Saudi Arabia has its own version of political Islam — state Wahhabism — and oscillates between repressing and co-opting the Brotherhood according to circumstance. Qatar, at the opposite extreme, actively finances it and uses it as an instrument of influence. The Emirates persecute it without quarter, in any country, under any flag. This obsession is the engine that explains why Abu Dhabi ends up supporting the same profiles of actors — secular military men, secessionist warlords, paramilitary forces — in conflicts as different as Libya, Yemen, Sudan and the Horn of Africa, and often in concert with Israel.

Dr Andreas Krieg, of King's College London, conceptualises it as the Emirati "axis of secessionists": a network of non-state actors — militias, paramilitaries, secessionist forces — operating as Abu Dhabi's advance guard in countries of strategic value. The mirror of Iran's "axis of resistance", but without religious rhetoric and with a more mercantile objective: to control the chokepoints of global trade. The aim is not to export an ideology. It is to export a favourable geography.

There is also another alignment underlying this whole architecture, one Saudi Arabia does not share in the same way: the relationship with Israel. No Gulf country has ties as deep with Tel Aviv as the UAE. They were not only among the principal drivers of the Abraham Accords; they also exchange intelligence, military equipment and surveillance technology as a matter of routine. That Abu Dhabi–Tel Aviv axis defines a vision of regional order — secular, anti-Islamist, transactionally pro-Western — that Riyadh never fully embraced, and which after 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza became even harder to sustain publicly.

One must be careful in the analysis. The fracture between Saudi Arabia and the UAE is not a rupture. It is the end of direct alignment and the beginning of open competition for primacy in the Arabian Peninsula. Historically, Saudi Arabia has held a dominant position in the Gulf Cooperation Council through its population, its economic size and its dominance in oil production. That is the status Abu Dhabi is trying to erode. But total schism is impossible: the tribal, religious, infrastructural and geographical relations between the Gulf countries are too dense to break. The failed attempt to blockade Qatar in 2017 — driven by MBZ and MBS themselves — is the best example of the limits of these strategies.
What exists, then, is not a war between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. It is a race. And that race can be seen in four conflicts that function as mirrors of the divergence.
Yemen: the port is the prize

The history of the conflict in Yemen is long and enormously complex, and it is not the first time Middle Eastern countries have intervened there with mixed results — the best-known case being Nasser's Egypt in the 1960s. In summary: the territory of Yemen contained two countries that unified in 1990 and which, after the Arab Spring, gave way to a rebellion by the Houthis — majority Shia clans loyal to the assassinated leader Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi. The movement overthrew the government in Sanaa, sought support from Iran and began threatening Saudi Arabia and the rest of the Gulf with drones. In consequence, Saudi Arabia and the UAE launched a joint operation in 2015 in support of the UN-recognised government. The operation did not achieve its objectives and ended in a modus vivendi among all the combatants.
But it is here that the divergence begins.

Saudi Arabia wanted to restore the government of Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi and, with it, a unified and manageable Yemen on its southern border. The Emirates wanted something else: the ports. Specifically, control of the southern coast — Aden, Mukalla, Balhaf — and the strategic position on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, through which around 10% of global maritime trade passes.

To achieve this, they financed and armed the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a secessionist force that does not recognise Hadi's government and functions as the Yemeni version of the Emirati strategy in other conflicts: a non-state actor that converts Abu Dhabi's interests into a plausible local cause. The STC not only controls Aden; it also allows Abu Dhabi Ports and DP World to manage, or aspire to manage, the southern port facilities. According to investigations by Middle East Eye and the UN panel of experts, the Emirati company also gains access to the energy infrastructure at Balhaf and to the Masila oilfields, whose crude reaches the global market through trader networks based in Dubai.

The fracture with Riyadh came in 2019, when the STC took Aden by force, defying the government Saudi Arabia was protecting. The Saudis accused the Emiratis of undermining the coalition. In December 2025, Saudi Arabia bombed what it described as an arms shipment destined for the Yemeni separatists backed by Abu Dhabi. It was not an accident. It was a message.

The Emirati logic is compelling: they do not need to win the war in Yemen. They need the STC to control the coast. That is enough. The irony of the outcome is that prolonging the conflict strengthened the Houthis sufficiently that, from 2023, their drone and missile attacks turned the Red Sea into a risk zone for global trade. The man who wanted to control the sea lanes contributed, in part, to someone else closing them first.
Sudan: gold and blood

The Sudanese case is clearer in its anatomy. After the coup that overthrew the brief post-Bashir democratic experiment, an alliance between the conventional Sudanese Army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) took power. The RSF are the formalisation and professionalisation of the Janjaweed militias — developed by the dictator Omar al-Bashir to repress and carry out ethnic cleansing in Darfur and in the conflict with South Sudan. Clashes over control of power led to the civil war of 2023.

The connection between Abu Dhabi and the RSF of Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, nicknamed "Hemeti", predates the conflict. During the Yemen campaign, the RSF sent thousands of fighters to serve under Emirati command — mercenaries who became a key source of income for Hemeti and allowed him to build an autonomous military apparatus within Sudan. The deal was simple: the Emirates paid in cash and trained; Hemeti gained regional projection.

What adds a second level is gold. Sudan is Africa's third largest gold producer. The RSF control much of the mining in Darfur and South Kordofan. According to investigations by Global Witness and the UN panel itself, that gold reaches the Emirates — specifically Dubai — refined and re-exported to the global market. Estimates exceed 90 tonnes a year over the 2017-2023 period, largely illegally. Dubai, which does not ask many questions, is the ideal hub.

The UAE also has other interests in the country: the purchase of land for agricultural exploitation, with the aim of providing food security for the Emirati population, and positions in the Sudanese oil export chain.

When civil war broke out in April 2023, Saudi Arabia and Egypt backed the internationally recognised government and the conventional army. Turkey did the same. The UAE stayed with Hemeti — officially denying it, but with solid journalistic documentation of arms shipments through Chad and the Central African Republic, using the same logistical networks that operated in Libya. The human result is devastating: more than eight million internally displaced people in 2024, the largest displacement crisis in the world, and scenes in Darfur that multiple bodies have characterised as genocide.

The Arab divergence in Sudan is the most revealing of all: Saudi Arabia wants a functional neighbour on the Red Sea. The UAE wants access to resources and coastlines, and that access does not require the Sudanese state to function.
Libya: the laboratory of the model

Libya was the first great experiment and where the Emirati script was codified. When Gaddafi fell in 2011, the UAE supported the NATO intervention alongside Qatar. While Doha bet on the Islamist militias and the Libyan arm of the Muslim Brotherhood, Abu Dhabi began looking for its own counter-figure.

They found him in Khalifa Haftar: a retired general, exiled in Virginia for decades, with anti-communist credentials and a ferocious animosity towards political Islam. The Emirates financed and armed him — in violation of the UN arms embargo — and supplied him with domestically manufactured drones that became the decisive weapon of his Libyan National Army (LNA). Krieg documents how Libya established the model that would be replicated in Yemen and Sudan: select a charismatic strongman, build a military apparatus and plausible political cover around him, and tie his existence to the Emirati financial and logistical network.

What the Libyan case also revealed was the Arab rift in all its dimensions. Qatar and Turkey financed the UN-recognised Government of National Accord, based in Tripoli. Saudi Arabia backed Haftar but more ambiguously. Egypt, whose relationship with Abu Dhabi has been one of near financial dependence since Sisi's 2013 coup — actively backed by the Emirates — sent materiel and, according to some reports, special forces. The result was a war of Arab proxies against Arabs, financed by petrodollars on both sides, that left Libya split in two and without a functioning state.

The fact that most discomfits Western analyses: according to the 2021 report of the UN panel of experts on Libya, the Emirati mercenary networks in the country were connected to Chadian fighters trained by Russia's Wagner Group, which was also operating in convergence with Abu Dhabi. The death of Chadian president Idriss Déby was carried out by rebels trained in Libya on payrolls issued by the United Arab Emirates. The geography of chaos Abu Dhabi propagates does not respect borders.
Somaliland: the port that recognises without recognising
If the three previous cases are wars, Somaliland is the most elegant version of the Emirati strategy: conquest without firing a shot.

Somaliland is a de facto state in northwestern Somalia. It declared independence in 1991, holds regular elections, has its own currency and organised armed forces. No state in the world formally recognises it. Abu Dhabi does not care.

In 2016, DP World — the Emirati government's port company — signed a 30-year concession agreement with Somaliland to develop the Port of Berbera for 442 million dollars. Berbera has an extraordinary geographical position: facing the Gulf of Aden, at strategic distance from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and positioned to become the alternative to the Port of Djibouti for Ethiopia — 125 million inhabitants who depend on that single access to the sea for more than 90% of their foreign trade. In 2018, Ethiopia joined the agreement by acquiring a 19% stake.

The academics Brendon Cannon and Ash Rossiter documented how Ethiopia actively manoeuvred to divert Emirati attention from Eritrea — where the UAE had a military base at Assab since 2015 — towards Berbera. Djibouti responded by nationalising the terminal DP World operated there and handing it to a Chinese operator. The move revealed clearly what was at stake: control of the gateway to the Horn of Africa, one of the busiest regions on the planet in terms of maritime traffic.

The UAE also has a military presence in the territory — a training base for Somaliland's forces — without having signed any defence treaty with any recognised state. They do not need to. What Somaliland gives them is exactly what they seek in each of their theatres: access to strategic coastlines without the burden of managing the internal politics of the country that hosts them. Informal recognition is enough. Real control, more than enough.

Here too there is a philosophical difference with Saudi Arabia, which speaks to the two models of regional power. Riyadh needs state structures that underwrite diplomatic contracts, long-term investments and conventional relationships. Abu Dhabi operates comfortably in the grey space between existence and non-existence. Failed states, unrecognised territories, zones of frozen war: that is its natural habitat.
The big brother no longer commands

In the final weeks of 2025, Saudi Arabia bombed what it described as an arms shipment bound for the Yemeni separatists backed by Abu Dhabi. It was not an accident. It was a message. The alliance the two countries had forged around the war against the Houthis — a war that, ironically, also united them against Iran — broke. Riyadh was trying to consolidate two states in Yemen; the UAE appeared to be seeking a more diffuse power arrangement and control of the country's ports through its allies.

The fracture has a precise geometry. Faced with Operation Epic Fury and the death of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in the first bombardments, Riyadh opted for a strategic pause. MBS watches today paralysed: the closure of Hormuz threatens the heart of his Vision 2030, which depends on stable exports and on presenting the kingdom as a world-class logistical and financial hub. A prolonged interruption of the Strait is not a setback; it is an existential crisis for the Saudi model.

Abu Dhabi took the opposite direction. The Emirates took hits from Iranian missiles. Dubai international airport was struck by a drone on 16 March, causing a fire in a fuel tank and a global disruption of air traffic. MBZ demands reparations, the unconditional reopening of Hormuz and what internal documents describe as "a comprehensive rollback of Iranian power." This is not the rhetoric of someone seeking a deal. It is the position of someone who wants to redesign the regional architecture from scratch.
"Abu Dhabi has concluded that its interests are better served acting as a sovereign actor than as a member of a cartel."
— Amir Handjani, Quincy Institute / Foreign Policy

The OPEC exit was not improvised in two weeks. It was built over two decades. The Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline, connecting the eastern fields with the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, is the backbone of the Emirati strategy of maritime independence. Under normal conditions it allows the export of 1.7 million barrels a day while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. It is, in strategic terms, the only real bypass for Gulf producers. Saudi Arabia has Yanbu on the Red Sea, but its capacity is lower and it depends on the Houthis not reaching further. The UAE has Fujairah.

The problem is one of scale: 1.7 million barrels is not enough. The UAE's installed capacity is 4.8 million. The gap — more than 3 million barrels trapped east of the Strait — explains both the urgency of the exit and the long-term bet. MBZ is not playing for this quarter. He is betting that, when Hormuz reopens and the UAE can release its full capacity, its position as an independent exporter — without the straitjacket of quotas — makes it the marginal arbiter of the global crude market.

There is a context that complicates this calculation: the UAE had a history of exceeding its own OPEC quotas, and the cartel, even in its OPEC+ form, was becoming ever less relevant as the sole arbiter of the global market. The North American shale revolution and the emergence of new producers — Guyana, Brazil, Argentina, Canada — left the cartel without the capacity to set prices on its own. Leaving an institution that no longer commands carries a political cost, but not a market one.
The bigger wave

There is a temptation to read the Emirates' OPEC exit as the definitive gesture of a state that has reached its strategic maturity. The small emirate that in 1971 barely existed as a coherent political unit today has the most strategic maritime corridor in the Gulf, the most sophisticated technological alliance with Israel in the Arab world, the most internationalised financial system in the region and, now, the capacity to produce oil without asking anyone's permission.

But the architecture has cracks of its own. In Sudan, support for the RSF left it on the wrong side of what multiple UN bodies characterise as genocide — with no possibility of plausible distance. In Libya, the proliferation of Emirati weapons fed the Sahel and contributed, in a documented chain, to the death of Chadian president Idriss Déby. In Yemen, the indirect strengthening of the Houthis, as a consequence of a conflict without political solution, ended up closing, at least partially, the very sea lanes over which Abu Dhabi had built its strategy of control.

The most lucid analysts warn that the very architecture that makes the UAE apparently invulnerable — networks of militias, financial dependencies, presence in five simultaneous theatres, the logic of a state that can coordinate operations in Sudan from an air-conditioned office in Dubai — is, by nature, difficult to sustain over time. When collective institutions fall, the vacuum is not filled by the most skilful actor: it is filled by entropy.

MBZ has decided, once again, that the risk of not going is greater than the risk of falling. He has paddled out while everyone else watched the storm from the shore. The Strait of Hormuz remains closed. Iran negotiates its collapse. Saudi Arabia recalculates its economic geography. And the Emirates, with their quota consigned to the drawer of history and their engineers watching the production models, wait for the moment when the water calms again to extract as much as they can from their crude output.
The question is not whether the wave exists. The question is whether anyone can surf a wave of those dimensions without taking the whole system down with them.
